Story

Why a house with a fish inside it

The meaning behind the mark, and the position it has to earn.

Uokura (魚蔵) literally means fish storehouse — a building built for one purpose: to hold something worth keeping. The mark is that building, drawn as a pagoda-roofed house with a fish held inside it. House and fish share the same roofline stroke on purpose — the restaurant isn't a fish shop that happens to have a dining room, it's a home for fish.

That reading isn't decoration — it's the actual site. Uokura runs out of a converted house in a Golden neighborhood, sushi-bar seating and all. The mark just tells guests, before they read a word of copy, what kind of place they're walking into.

It also sets the brand's real job. The research behind this project found a loyal base that already believes this ("hidden gem," "our go-to," "if you know you know" — outnumbering first-timer language 3.45 to 1 in the reviews) sitting next to a shrinking discovery funnel (review volume down 37% from its 2019 peak). The identity's work isn't to convince regulars — they're already convinced. It's to make the storehouse findable.

"it's still just as good as the first time i went, 15 years ago"5★, Local Guide — Google review of Sushi Uokura
Logo system

The mark

Primary mark, clear space, minimum sizes, and what never to do to it.

Primary — red on light surfaces
Mono — white, for navy or photographic backgrounds
Mono — navy, for single-color print (menus, stamps, embroidery)

Clear space & minimum size

Clear space≥ the height of the fish motif, measured on all four sides. Nothing — text, edges, other marks — enters that zone.
Minimum size — digital28px tall. Below that, drop to the wordmark alone.
Minimum size — print0.35in / 9mm tall.
Favicon cropSquare crop to the mark's bounding box, ~12% padding. See tab mock below.

Voice & tone

Sound like a regular, not a chain

Five rules, grounded in what actually shows up in a decade of reviews.

Do
Say plainly what AYCE includes — nigiri, rolls, and appetizers made fresh per order.
Don't
Let "all you can eat" imply an unlimited menu. 31% of reviews mention AYCE, and several cite exactly this mismatch.
Do
Name the fish — Uokura Roll, maguro, uni, the actual dish.
Don't
Default to "delicious sushi." The signature Uokura Roll appears in just 2 of 790 reviews — specificity is unclaimed territory.
Do
Say "call to reserve" and mean it.
Don't
Promise "book online" — there's no live booking system, and implying one creates the exact kind of broken expectation the phone-and-voicemail reviews already describe.
Do
Address parking head-on, helpfully, before anyone has to ask.
Don't
Stay silent on it. It's the single most-repeated complaint, including guests who left without eating.
Do
Write like you're telling a neighbor where to eat.
Don't
Reach for "elevated culinary experience" language. The brand's real asset is "if you know you know" — protect that, don't polish it away.

Imagery

Photography direction

The brief for Session 09's food photography — only shot with the owner's own reference photos and permission.

Light

Natural window light, no on-camera flash. Matches the converted-house intimacy — nothing should look like a studio.

Angle

Close, slightly above the plate, shallow depth of field. One dish holds focus; the rest of the table falls soft.

Props

Dark slate or unfinished wood surfaces. No overstyled garnish — the plate should look like what actually arrives at the table.

Color

Let the fish read true. Avoid warm filters that push salmon toward neon-orange — accuracy over Instagram gloss.

Must-haves

At least one shot of the sushi-bar seating (the intimacy is a real strength) and one exterior shot of the house, addressing "where do I park" before anyone has to ask.

Mark placement

Where a mark appears in-frame (chopstick sleeve, plate edge), use the navy mono version — the red stays reserved for the digital brand, not competing with the food's own red tones.

Canonical tokens ship in brand/tokens.css — Session 07 imports the variable names above verbatim, no renaming.
